set.approach: From the West Portal (East Inlet) trailhead near Grand Lake, follow the trail along the north side of East Inlet; a meadow early on is one of the few places the ice can be spotted. The trail then gains height to a viewpoint, drops into the valley floor and turns north along the base of Mt Craig, running past the Gray Jay group site. For the hidden amphitheater, leave the trail beyond the second bridge, before the privy, and contour up and around the prominent rock band to a short narrow gully and a boulderfield, where the ice comes into view. Snow is often deep, so snowshoes and an early start help, and the slopes above and below carry serious avalanche exposure: check the avalanche forecast.
set.descent_text: Rappel from the stout bush with slings near the top of the route, well above the steep ice, using long ropes since the line is steep and fairly smooth.

review.notes: Area page for trailhead/approach and amphitheater location; route page for the bush anchor. Rope/rappel counts left out (single source).

set.descent_text: Rappel the route from screws or V-threads, or better, from the large bush with slings reached by traversing right and up near the top of the second pitch. The first-pitch belay ledge has tree anchors that are also used to rappel from.

review.notes: Route page for the anchors and ledges; area page for approach.

The trail then gains height to a viewpoint, drops into the valley floor and turns north along the base of Mt Craig, running past the Gray Jay group site. The route is the furthest-left flow inside that same bowl, beside Tunnel Vision.
set.descent_text: From the top you can climb on into the upper part of Tunnel Vision and descend that way. Otherwise wade through bushes to a tree on the left and rappel to the big ledge, then rappel again down the lower ice. Ropes do not quite reach the ground from the lower belay, so downclimb the last few feet on the left.

review.notes: Route page for the two descent options.

set.approach: From the West Portal (East Inlet) trailhead near Grand Lake, follow the trail along the north side of East Inlet; a meadow early on is one of the few places the ice can be spotted. The trail then gains height to a viewpoint, drops into the valley floor and turns north along the base of Mt Craig, running past the Gray Jay group site. This line sits on the northwest side of the mountain by the upper end of Lone Pine Lake, a short walk from the main trail and not far up-valley from the Gray Jay group site. The last stretch off the trail can be a deep-snow wallow. Avalanche terrain is nearby: check the avalanche forecast.
set.descent_text: Rappel from a large tree with slings and rings at the top of the route onto a gentler snowy patch with more trees, then rappel again to the base.

review.notes: Route page: location by Lone Pine Lake and the tree rappels.

set.approach: From the West Portal (East Inlet) trailhead near Grand Lake, follow the trail along the north side of East Inlet; a meadow early on is one of the few places the ice can be spotted. The trail then gains height to a viewpoint, drops into the valley floor and turns north along the base of Mt Craig, running past the Gray Jay group site. This is the nearest of the Craig ice lines to the trailhead: a yellowish flow where a prominent gully facing west ends, several hundred yards south of the main amphitheater, and it can be glimpsed from the meadow and between trees. The last approach through deep snow can be hard work. Avalanche terrain: check the avalanche forecast.

review.notes: Approach only; no descent stated on the page.

set.approach: Access is from the signed Middle Fork turnoff south of Silver Jack Reservoir. In winter the road is not plowed this far, so reaching the ice usually means a long ski or walk, or a snowmobile. This flow is close to the Middle Fork Road. Park at a small clearing on the left, hike south through the trees and turn east into the first drainage; the falls sit in a scenic alcove a few minutes up.
set.descent_text: Several trees above and to the left of the top-out are slung for rappelling.

set.approach: Access is from the signed Middle Fork turnoff south of Silver Jack Reservoir. In winter the road is not plowed this far, so reaching the ice usually means a long ski or walk, or a snowmobile. This flow is close to the Middle Fork Road. Park at the same small clearing as for Big Green Falls, take the use trail north through the trees, then head east up the first drainage; the flow is visible within a few minutes.
set.descent_text: Just above the steep section, a two-bolt anchor sits on the left in the rock-walled gully. Easy ice continues above, and parties walk back down beside the flow to the bolts.

set.approach: Access is from the signed Middle Fork turnoff south of Silver Jack Reservoir. In winter the road is not plowed this far, so reaching the ice usually means a long ski or walk, or a snowmobile. This flow is close to the Middle Fork Road. Park at a pullout on the right at a drainage a few drainages north of the Big Green Falls clearing, then bushwhack east up it; the ice is hidden until you are right below it, tucked into a corner where the stream drops over a cliff.
set.descent_text: A sturdy willow at the top is the anchor; the pitch is taller than it looks, so check that your rope will reach before lowering or rappelling.

review.notes: Route page; rope length uncertain on the page, so not stated.

set.approach: Access is from the signed Middle Fork turnoff south of Silver Jack Reservoir. In winter the road is not plowed this far, so reaching the ice usually means a long ski or walk, or a snowmobile. This flow is close to the Middle Fork Road. Park at a small pullout on the right at the second drainage north of the Frost Giant clearing and hike east up the drainage to the ice.
set.descent_text: Rappel short pitches off trees, or traverse north to the adjacent drainage (Screwed Once Again) and rappel the larger flow there from the existing anchor.

review.notes: Route page; neighbouring page confirms the anchor in the next drainage.

set.approach: Access is from the signed Middle Fork turnoff south of Silver Jack Reservoir. In winter the road is not plowed this far, so reaching the ice usually means a long ski or walk, or a snowmobile. This flow is close to the Middle Fork Road. Park near the drainage on the right, the third north of the Frost Giant clearing, and hike east up it to the ice; a second short route lies in the willowy gully to the left.
set.descent_text: A cluster of trees at the top holds an anchor, and a fixed anchor is also reported at the top of this flow for rappelling.

review.notes: Both pages mention an anchor at the top.

set.approach: Access is from the signed Middle Fork turnoff south of Silver Jack Reservoir. In winter the road is not plowed this far, so reaching the ice usually means a long ski or walk, or a snowmobile. This flow is close to the Middle Fork Road. Park at the same small pullout as for Blue-Headed Stepchild, cross the creek heading west-northwest, and follow the easiest line to a cliff band in a northeast-facing drainage.
set.descent_text: Rappel from willows at the top, or walk off to the left.

set.approach: From the Middle Fork trailhead follow the trail up the valley to below the obvious Precipice Amphitheater East, which usually holds many ice flows. Ford the river and angle uphill westward to the ice-filled bowl. After November the approach is a long ski or hike from the winter parking near Silver Jack unless you have a snowmobile. Avalanche paths from the north face of Precipice and the southeast face of Dunsinane meet above and on the approach: check the avalanche forecast. The route is the flagship pillar in the amphitheater, rising from a wide slab.

From the Middle Fork trailhead follow the trail up the valley to below the obvious Precipice Amphitheater East, which usually holds many ice flows. Ford the river and angle uphill westward to the ice-filled bowl. After November the approach is a long ski or hike from the winter parking near Silver Jack unless you have a snowmobile. Avalanche paths from the north face of Precipice and the southeast face of Dunsinane meet above and on the approach: check the avalanche forecast. This is the large flow to the right of the Giant pillar.
set.descent_text: V-thread off the top with long ropes. Avalanche hazard exists above the climb as well as on the approach.

set.approach: From the Middle Fork trailhead follow the trail up the valley to below the obvious Precipice Amphitheater East, which usually holds many ice flows. Ford the river and angle uphill westward to the ice-filled bowl. After November the approach is a long ski or hike from the winter parking near Silver Jack unless you have a snowmobile. Avalanche paths from the north face of Precipice and the southeast face of Dunsinane meet above and on the approach: check the avalanche forecast. The route starts lower in the amphitheater, to the left of the Giant pillar.
set.descent_text: Descend by rappelling off trees, V-threads or boulders, using doubled ropes.

set.approach: From the Middle Fork trailhead, follow the trail up the valley to where it meets the drainage below the climb, then scout the pillar by peering east between the trees and hike up the drainage to it. After November it is a long ski or hike from the winter parking near Silver Jack unless you have a snowmobile. A large bowl empties onto the climb: check the avalanche forecast.

From the Middle Fork trailhead, follow the trail (or the river when it is snow-covered) up the valley past the drainage leading to Silence, spot a break in the forest to the southwest and follow the drainage above it to the column. The flow collects runoff from Precipice Peak's east side, and below the basalt dike you stand in a large funnel exposed to slides from several directions: check the avalanche forecast.
set.descent_text: Anchor below the lip, or climb the easing ice and steep snow above to a cluster of small trees. V-threads are the best way down if the ice allows; otherwise rappel from the trees.

set.approach: Follow the Middle Fork trail up the valley until Precipice Peak shows a yellow smear high to the southwest, continue a bit farther to a nondescript drainage on the west side, leave the trail, cross the river and climb the drainage; a minor WI2 step midway can be skirted on its right, and the final grovel is awkward when snow is thin. Avalanche terrain: check the avalanche forecast.
set.descent_text: Belay or anchor in the bulge before the ice ends, or hike up to the abrupt ridge and look for a skinny bush or crumbly knob. Rappel all the way to the base with long ropes, or rappel to the pocket and downclimb from there.

set.approach: From the Middle Fork trailhead follow the main trail to the signed junction for Porphyry Basin, then leave it and scramble up the streambed, passing a few short ice steps on the way to the falls. If the creek is not frozen there is probably no ice on the falls.
set.descent_text: Scramble out of the creek toward the north to meet the Porphyry Basin trail, which leads back down to the Middle Fork trail.

set.approach: From the Middle Fork trailhead follow the trail to the signed Porphyry Basin junction. Leave the trail there, contour southwest, cross the Middle Fork River and pick up the next drainage to the west. Follow it southwest to a fork, take the left (south) fork, and at the next fork go right (north) due west into the alcove that holds the smear.
set.descent_text: Anchor before the ice ends, or climb the loose slope above to the nearest tree and rappel from it to a platform, then downclimb or make a short V-thread rappel to the creek bottom.

set.approach: Walk the Middle Fork trail a long way up the valley to where the flow shows in a northeast-facing drainage on Redcliff. Step off the trail, go over the meadow and work uphill by the easiest ground. It is a very long way from anywhere a vehicle can reach in winter.
set.descent_text: Trees to the left of the top-out hold the anchor. The preferred way down is to walk off toward the east or southeast, though rappelling works too.

set.approach: Go north from Pagosa Springs on Piedra Road (CR 600), then bear right on FS 636 toward Middle Fork to the parking area. In winter the road beyond is groomed for snowmobiles and the final miles to the Middle Fork trailhead are covered by ski, foot or sled. From the trailhead head northeast to the river and follow it up the canyon, which can be quick or tedious depending on snow and how frozen the river is, to the junction with Lean Creek. Turn up the Lean Creek drainage and walk a short way to the ice.

review.notes: Area page for road; route page for canyon walk. This area is the Middle Fork of the Piedra River near Pagosa Springs.

set.approach: Go north from Pagosa Springs on Piedra Road (CR 600), then bear right on FS 636 toward Middle Fork to the parking area. In winter the road beyond is groomed for snowmobiles and the final miles to the Middle Fork trailhead are covered by ski, foot or sled. From the trailhead head northeast to the river and follow it up the canyon, which can be quick or tedious depending on snow and how frozen the river is, to the junction with Lean Creek. Head right up Lean Creek to the thin smear to the left of Lean Creek Falls.
set.descent_text: V-thread off the bulge at the top, or carry gear and top out.

set.approach: Go north from Pagosa Springs on Piedra Road (CR 600), then bear right on FS 636 toward Middle Fork to the parking area. In winter the road beyond is groomed for snowmobiles and the final miles to the Middle Fork trailhead are covered by ski, foot or sled. From the trailhead head northeast to the river and follow it up the canyon, which can be quick or tedious depending on snow and how frozen the river is, to the junction with Lean Creek. Instead of turning up Lean Creek, carry on up the Middle Fork a few minutes and cut right to the flow on the canyon's east side.
set.descent_text: Rappel from chockstones above and left of the top-out. They may not be there, so plan to build your own anchor.

set.approach: From the northeast end of Silverton take County Road 2 toward Eureka and turn at the signed Minnie Gulch junction, then follow the gulch road up. The gully is very obvious on the right side of the road. The road is usually snowed in by mid-winter, so later in the season expect a ski or walk along it.

review.notes: Area page and route page. No descent stated.

set.approach: From the northeast end of Silverton take County Road 2 toward Eureka and turn at the signed Minnie Gulch junction, then follow the gulch road up. About halfway along, the route lies across the valley on the right, directly opposite a high-flow waterfall. The road is usually snowed in by mid-winter, so later in the season expect a ski or walk along it.

review.notes: Area page and route page. No descent stated.

set.approach: Mount Kennedy lies deep in the Weminuche Wilderness. Reach it by the Durango and Silverton train to Needleton, or by the Purgatory Flats trail (#511), then take the Needle Creek trail (#504) south toward Chicago Basin to the point where it runs beneath the peak's big north buttress, a spot with places to camp. From the trail cross Needle Creek, possibly on downed trees, and aim for the shallow drainage between the willows and the timber east of the clearing below the face, then follow the easiest line up to the snow at the base of the couloir.
set.descent_text: From the crest above the couloir the summit is a short walk to the left. The way down is the wide gully on the north side, just east of the summit.

review.notes: Area page for trail approach; route page for the approach and descent.

set.approach: From Exit 240 on I-70 west of Idaho Springs, drive to the town of Alice and take the dirt Alice Road to a small pullout with a trailhead sign. The trail leads up to Loch Lomond, above which the East Ridge Direct begins. From the base of that ridge, head right to the buttress to the north and find the gully that falls from the notch where the East Ridge is hardest; the route follows the diagonal ramp just left of it.
set.descent_text: The route joins the ridge and follows it to the summit. The southeast ridge is the usual way down and is a Class 2 walk.

review.notes: Area and route pages. Trail to Loch Lomond inferred from East Ridge Direct page saying it starts above the lake.

set.approach: From Exit 240 on I-70 west of Idaho Springs, drive to the town of Alice and take the dirt Alice Road to a small pullout with a trailhead sign. Follow the path to Loch Lomond, then continue toward the East Ridge Direct. Instead of heading right toward that ridge, look left for the obvious big black chockstone that gives the route its name. Deep snow can make this stretch very slow. Check the avalanche forecast.

review.notes: Approach only; descent options not clearly stated (rappel or continue).

set.approach: The route is reached from the Black Wall raps, so the usual way in is from the top, by rappelling to the snowfield at the foot of the wall; a long approach from the Guanella Pass side is also possible. Be sure to head for the gully, not the start of the neighbouring route Good Evans; the line goes up the rightmost corner, which begins as a turfy ramp.

The route shares its lower section with Black and White, so the access is the same: reach the Black Wall by rappelling in from above or by a long approach from the Guanella Pass side, then climb the lower pitches of that route before staying in the main gully system.

The line takes the left side of the gully splitting the Black Wall, starting at the bottom of the rappels down the wall, and is marked by free-hanging icicles. Access is by rappelling the wall from the top.

It follows the steep chimney system on the left side of Silhouette. Access is by climbing the neighbouring route Monochrome into it, by traversing over from the start of Silhouette, or, if the lower face holds little ice, by rappelling in to the base.

Reach the base either by climbing the first pitch of Silhouette or by going down into the base along the wall's left flank when the lower smears are not in shape. The line of the ghostly icicle left of Shooting Star is hard to miss.

Drive to the summit parking lot and walk up the trail to the notch below the summit, then descend the slanting snow band toward the northeast until you are under the route; it is a short, easy approach. The start is beside the upper couloir of The Snave, on its left, at a small tongue of snow leading to an icy dihedral capped by a flake.

Park at Summit Lake and take the broad trail toward the notch facing the Tan Buttresses, then drop down and left into the cirque. Continue to the foot of the first buttress on your left; the route is one of several gullies, on the right side of the buttress, a parallel-sided gully with a steep chimney higher up. The approach is short and downhill.

Park at Summit Lake and take the broad trail toward the notch facing the Tan Buttresses, then drop down and left into the cirque and below the first buttress on the left. The route takes the right-most of the gullies, one gully right of Mount Evans Micro Goulotte, marked by a prominent right-facing fin. The approach is short and downhill.

Park at Summit Lake and take the broad trail toward the notch facing the Tan Buttresses, then drop into the cirque. The route is the right-hand gully of a twin gully system, uphill of and to the climber's right of Snorkmaiden's Surprise.
set.descent_text: The gully tops out on the hikers' trail that leads to Mt Spaulding; follow that trail back to the Chicago Lakes Overlook.

review.notes: Route page for descent; neighbouring page for approach to the adjacent gully.

set.approach: Drive to the summit road's end and rappel from the high point itself, which carries the benchmark pin, down the line of the route to the snow-covered ramp seen below. From the ramp the climb goes back up the same line.

From the Summit Lake trailhead go southwest into the Summit Lake bowl just below the face, then climb steep snow south to the base of the main summit block. The route then traverses left below the lower cliff band toward the couloir.

review.notes: Area page for the approach to the bowl; route page for the start of the route. No descent stated.

co_mt_blue_sky_formerly_mount_evans_mixe.skip_reason: Page gives no approach and only a one-page mid-couloir rappel; left unwritten rather than guess.
